name: Tessera Corponation Distributed Reflex Mesh
description:
The Distributed Reflex Mesh is a subcutaneous augmentation network consisting of several hundred microscopic bioelectric relay nodes implanted across the body's major muscle groups via injection-based deployment. Unlike conventional reflex augmentations that enhance the speed of the central nervous system's command-and-response loop, the Mesh operates on a fundamentally different architectural principle: it creates a secondary, decentralized reflex network that allows localized muscle groups to respond to immediate physical stimuli — impact, blade contact, electrical discharge — without waiting for the signal to complete a round trip to the brain and back. Each node cluster communicates laterally with adjacent nodes and with local muscle tissue, enabling what Tessera's documentation describes as 'distributed somatic response' — essentially, parts of the body can flinch, brace, or reposition faster than conscious awareness allows because they are acting on local signal processing rather than central command.

Tessera developed the Mesh as a defensive augmentation rather than an offensive one, and this distinction shapes its entire design philosophy. It does not make users faster at initiating movement — their reaction time for deliberate actions is unchanged. What it does is make the body significantly better at protecting itself from things the user didn't see coming. A strike to an unguarded flank triggers a local bracing response in the struck muscle group within milliseconds; a hand moving toward a hot surface retracts before the pain signal fully registers; a stumble on uneven ground is corrected by automatic micro-adjustments in posture before the user consciously registers the imbalance. The cumulative effect is a body that is much harder to damage through the attacks that conventional reflexes miss — the sucker punch, the environmental hazard, the stumble in a firefight.

The injection deployment method means installation can be performed in under two hours in a reasonably equipped medical facility, with no recovery time beyond mild diffuse soreness for forty-eight hours. This ease of deployment has made the Mesh popular across a wide range of users who want meaningful augmentation without extended surgical downtime. The decentralized architecture also makes the Mesh unusually resilient — destroying or disrupting individual nodes has minimal effect on overall function, and the network self-reconfigures around damaged areas.

cultural_context: The Distributed Reflex Mesh has achieved broad adoption across Meridian 88's professional risk community precisely because of its low barrier to installation and its defensive rather than offensive character. Many employers who restrict offensive augmentations permit or even encourage the Mesh, reasoning that an augmentation that protects rather than empowers is a reasonable workplace safety measure. This has created an interesting social stratification: the Mesh is common enough that its absence is sometimes read as a signal of either poverty or deliberate ideological choice. Certain communities — particularly among the city's labor organizing movement — have adopted a norm of refusing all augmentation including the Mesh as a statement against the creeping expectation that workers should modify their bodies to perform dangerous jobs rather than demanding safer jobs.
known_users: Corporate security personnel across multiple tiers
Construction and industrial workers in hazardous environments
Couriers and delivery operators working contested routes
Field medics operating in active combat zones
Anyone who can afford Tier 2 augmentation and works in physical danger
story_hooks: Tessera Corponation has quietly pushed a firmware update to deployed Mesh networks that introduces a remote-disable function — someone has discovered this and is deciding whether to go public, knowing the information will create panic among the hundreds of thousands of Mesh users in the city.

A character's Mesh nodes are reaching end-of-life unevenly, creating zones of the body with degraded or absent coverage — they keep being surprised by injuries in areas they unconsciously believed were protected.

A new criminal organization has developed a weapon specifically designed to exploit the Mesh's local response protocol, triggering false-positive bracing responses to create openings in a target's guard — they are hunting Mesh users specifically.

An industrial accident has killed workers who were all wearing the Mesh — investigation suggests the distributed node network may have interfered with emergency equipment designed to detect worker vital signs, masking the distress signals that should have triggered an automated rescue response.
